To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the interpretation of amyloid and tau PET scans is not as simple as it may appear at first glance.

(1) The presence of amyloid PET positivity does not necessarily mean that a patient is in the preclinical AD stage, and (2) The presence of tau PET positivity does not always mean that a patient has AD.
amyloid and tau PET may be useful biomarkers in the preclinical and early stages of AD, but that the interpretation of PET results may not be as straightforward as it seems.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: 1) The development of novel methods to quantify the spatial distribution of PET data, 2) The development of new PET radiotracers to image tau pathology, and 3) the development of new methods to quantify the temporal evolution of tau pathology.
the use of biomarkers to predict the risk of AD in individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI).
the development of novel PET radiotracers for the imaging of tau and amyloid pathology in AD and other neurodegenerative disorders.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PET imaging is an important tool in the diagnosis of AD, and is a useful tool in the study of AD pathogenesis.
the sensitivity and specificity, as well as the clinical interpretation, of amyloid and tau PET are highly dependent on the location and the amount of the radiotrager in the brain.

amyloid PET imaging is a sensitive marker of the presence of brain Ab, but not a specific marker of AD; and tau PET is a sensitive marker for brain tangle pathology, but not a marker specific for AD, and the location of tau accumulation is critical for its interpretation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

amyloid PET has been very useful in identifying individuals with brain amyloid, and that tau PET has been very helpful in identifying individuals with tau deposition in the neocortex, but that neither of these tracers are perfect.
PET is a very powerful tool for diagnosis, staging, and treatment response, but it is not a "magic bullet."

we have found that the presence of amyloid is associated with the presence of tau, that the location of the tau may be more predictive of the clinical presentation, and that the presence of tau in the medial temporal lobe is not necessarily associated with the presence or severity of dementia.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sensitivity and specificity for AD of PET biomarkers may not be as high as previously thought.
, in the absence of a gold standard, we need to be careful in our interpretation of PET data.

the sensitivity and specificity (or positive and negative predictive values) of amyloid and tau PET in AD is dependent on clinical stage, the location of the pathology, the type of pathology, and the threshold for defining a positive or a negative scan.
